questions.question: What is Docker and what problem does it solve?
questions.answer: Docker packages an application and its dependencies into a container — a lightweight, portable, isolated unit. Solves: 'works on my machine' problem, dependency conflicts, environment inconsistency. Containers share the host OS kernel (unlike VMs which need a full OS). Consistent from dev laptop to production.

questions.question: What is the difference between a container and a virtual machine?
questions.answer: VM: full OS per VM, hypervisor, gigabytes, minutes to start. Container: shared kernel, namespaces+cgroups for isolation, megabytes, seconds to start. VMs: stronger isolation (separate kernel). Containers: faster, lighter, better density. Use both: VMs for infra isolation, containers for application isolation.

questions.question: What are Linux namespaces and how do they enable containers?
questions.answer: Namespaces isolate: pid (process IDs), net (networking), mnt (filesystem mounts), uts (hostname), ipc (inter-process comms), user (user IDs). Each container gets its own set of namespaces — sees isolated view of the system. Docker creates namespaces per container via clone() syscall.

questions.question: What are cgroups and what do they control?
questions.answer: Control Groups: Linux kernel feature limiting resource usage per process group. Docker uses cgroups to enforce: CPU limits/shares, memory limits (triggers OOMKill when exceeded), disk I/O throttling, network bandwidth. Without cgroups: one container could starve all others on the host.

questions.question: What is the Docker daemon and Docker client?
questions.answer: Daemon (dockerd): background service managing containers, images, networks, volumes. Listens on Unix socket (/var/run/docker.sock). Client (docker CLI): sends commands to daemon via REST API over the socket. They can run on different machines (remote daemon). Docker Desktop bundles both.

questions.question: What is the container lifecycle?
questions.answer:
Created → Running → Paused → Stopped → Deleted.
- First command: creates container, doesn't start.
- Second command: starts existing container.
- Third command: create + start in one command.
- Fourth command: SIGTERM then SIGKILL after timeout.
- Fifth command: immediate SIGKILL.
- Sixth command: removes stopped container.

questions.question: What is the difference between docker run and docker exec?
questions.answer: First command: creates and starts a new container from an image. Second command: runs a command inside an already-running container. Use the third command for debugging. Exec process shares the container's namespaces — same network, filesystem, PIDs.

questions.question: What is a Docker image and how does it differ from a container?
questions.answer: Image: read-only template — layered filesystem snapshot. Container: running instance of an image — adds a writable layer on top. Multiple containers from the same image share read-only layers. Deleting a container doesn't delete the image. The following command creates new image from container state (avoid in production).

questions.question: What is the Docker registry and how does push/pull work?
questions.answer: Registry: server storing Docker images. Docker Hub: default public registry. ECR, GCR, ACR: cloud private registries. First command downloads layers not already cached. Second command uploads layers to registry. Tags: image:latest is default but misleading — always use explicit version tags in production.
bestPractices: Always use explicit version tags in production instead of image:latest.

questions.question: What is containerd and how does it relate to Docker?
questions.answer: containerd: industry-standard container runtime (CNCF project). Docker originally used its own runtime, now delegates to containerd. Kubernetes uses containerd directly (via CRI) — doesn't need Docker. containerd manages: image pull, container lifecycle, snapshots. runc: low-level OCI runtime that containerd uses to actually create containers.

questions.question: What is a Dockerfile and what are the most important instructions?
questions.answer: Text file with instructions to build an image. Key: FROM (base image), RUN (execute command, creates layer), COPY/ADD (add files), ENV (env vars), EXPOSE (document port), CMD (default command), ENTRYPOINT (fixed executable), WORKDIR (set working dir), ARG (build-time variable), USER (run as user).

questions.question: What is the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT?
questions.answer: ENTRYPOINT: defines the executable — always runs, not overridable with the arguments of the first command. CMD: default arguments to ENTRYPOINT, or default command if no ENTRYPOINT — overridable with the arguments of the first command. Best practice: ENTRYPOINT for the executable, CMD for default args. Exec form preferred: the following instruction.
bestPractices: Use ENTRYPOINT for the executable and CMD for default arguments.
Prefer the exec form of instructions.

questions.question: What is the difference between COPY and ADD?
questions.answer: COPY: simply copies files from build context to image — prefer this. ADD: copies files AND auto-extracts tar archives AND supports URLs — too much magic, use only when you need tar extraction. Best practice: use COPY always unless you specifically need ADD's tar extraction behaviour.
bestPractices: Use COPY always unless you specifically need ADD's tar extraction behaviour.

questions.question: What is a multi-stage build and why is it important?
questions.answer: Multiple FROM statements in one Dockerfile. Build stage: compile, install dev dependencies, run tests. Final stage: COPY only the artifact from build stage — no compiler, no dev deps, no source code. Result: tiny production image. Example: Node.js builder 800MB → final 80MB. Security: smaller attack surface.

questions.question: How do Docker image layers work?
questions.answer: Each instruction that modifies filesystem creates a new layer. Layers are cached — unchanged layers reuse cache. Order matters: put rarely-changing instructions first (such as the first two instructions), frequently-changing last (such as the third instruction). Layer cache invalidated if any earlier layer changes. Improves build speed dramatically.
bestPractices: Put rarely-changing instructions first, frequently-changing last to leverage caching.

questions.question: How do you optimise a Dockerfile for layer caching?
questions.answer: Order: FROM → system deps (rarely change) → app deps (the package.json COPY + the npm install command) → source code (frequently changes). Group RUN commands: the following command. Never split apt-get update and apt-get install — cache stale deps risk.

codeBlocks.code: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y pkg1 pkg2 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

bestPractices: Group RUN commands to minimize layer count.
Order instructions: base image -> system deps -> app deps -> source code.
warnings: Never split apt-get update and apt-get install due to cache stale dependencies risk.

questions.question: What is .dockerignore and why does it matter?
questions.answer: Like .gitignore for Docker build context. Excludes files sent to daemon during build. Exclude: .git, node_modules, test files, logs, local config. Benefits: faster builds (less context to send), smaller images (fewer files copied), security (don't accidentally COPY secrets). Always create .dockerignore for every project.
bestPractices: Always create .dockerignore for every project to prevent copying build debris and secrets.

questions.question: What is the difference between ARG and ENV in Dockerfile?
questions.answer: ARG: build-time variable only — not available in running container. Set with the first option. ENV: runtime environment variable — available in container. ARG visible in the output of the second command — don't use for secrets. ENV persists in image — visible to anyone who inspects it. Neither is secure for secrets — use runtime secret injection.
warnings: ARG is visible in docker history and ENV persists in the image; neither is secure for secrets.

questions.question: What is the HEALTHCHECK instruction?
questions.answer: Defines a command Docker runs periodically to test container health. The first command shows health status: starting, healthy, unhealthy. The second instruction defines the check. Unhealthy containers kept running (Docker doesn't restart) but K8s liveness probe integration possible.

questions.question: How do you reduce Docker image size?
questions.answer: Use minimal base image (alpine, distroless, scratch). Multi-stage builds — copy only artifacts. Chain RUN commands — fewer layers, clean up in same RUN. Remove package manager caches (using the first two commands). Don't install unnecessary tools. Use .dockerignore. Regularly audit with the third command and the fourth tool.
bestPractices: Use minimal base images.
Chain RUN commands.
Remove package manager caches in the same layer.
Regularly audit with dive.

questions.question: What is a distroless image?
questions.answer: Images containing only the application and its runtime dependencies — no shell, no package manager, no OS utilities. Google maintains distroless images (gcr.io/distroless). Extremely small attack surface — no shell means no interactive exploitation. Harder to debug but excellent for production. Use multi-stage: build in full image, deploy in distroless.
bestPractices: Use multi-stage: build in full image, deploy in distroless.

questions.question: What is docker build cache and when does it get invalidated?
questions.answer: Cache valid if: same instruction, same base layer, same build context files for COPY/ADD. Invalidated by: any change to instruction text, file change in COPY/ADD, ARG change, the first flag. Once one layer invalidates, all subsequent layers also invalidate. Run the second instruction before the third instruction to preserve the fourth command's cache.

questions.question: What are Docker network drivers and when do you use each?
questions.answer: bridge (default): NAT-based, containers communicate by name on same network. host: container uses host network directly — no isolation, maximum performance. none: no networking. overlay: multi-host networking (Swarm/K8s). macvlan: container gets its own MAC address on physical network. Use bridge for most local dev, host for performance-critical tools.

questions.question: How does container-to-container communication work on a bridge network?
questions.answer: Containers on same user-defined bridge network: communicate by container name (DNS resolution). Default bridge network: containers communicate by IP only — no DNS. Always create user-defined bridge networks — never rely on default bridge. Run the first command then the second command.
bestPractices: Always create user-defined bridge networks; never rely on the default bridge network.

questions.question: What is port mapping (port publishing) in Docker?
questions.answer: Maps host port to container port: the first command (host:container). Only the mapped port is accessible from outside. Container can still reach other containers directly via internal IPs. The second parameter binds all interfaces. The third parameter binds localhost only (more secure). Exposed ports in Dockerfile are documentation only.
warnings: Exposed ports in Dockerfile are documentation only; they do not map ports automatically.

questions.question: How does Docker DNS work for service discovery?
questions.answer: Docker's embedded DNS server at 127.0.0.11. Containers on user-defined networks resolve other containers by name. Also resolves by service name in Compose. DNS returns container's internal IP. Works for: microservice discovery in dev, Compose service communication. In K8s: CoreDNS handles this instead.

questions.question: What is an overlay network?
questions.answer: Multi-host network spanning multiple Docker hosts (Swarm). Uses VXLAN encapsulation — container traffic tunneled between hosts. Containers on different hosts communicate by name as if local. Required for Docker Swarm. In K8s context: CNI plugins (Calico, Cilium) implement equivalent overlay functionality.

questions.question: How do you restrict container network access?
questions.answer: The first parameter: no networking at all. User-defined networks: containers only see other containers on same network — default deny across networks. iptables rules: Docker manages these automatically. In K8s: NetworkPolicy for pod-level control. The second command provides no external access. Principle: give containers only network access they need.
bestPractices: Give containers only the network access they absolutely need.

questions.question: What is host networking mode and when should you use it?
questions.answer: Container shares host's network namespace — no NAT, no port mapping needed. Use for: performance-critical workloads where NAT overhead matters, tools needing to monitor host network (like the first two commands), legacy apps hardcoded to specific ports. Security risk: container can access all host network interfaces. Avoid in production K8s (not supported on all platforms).
warnings: Security risk: container can access all host network interfaces in host networking mode.
Avoid in production K8s.

questions.question: How does Docker handle external DNS resolution for containers?
questions.answer: Container /etc/resolv.conf configured at runtime. Default: uses host's DNS settings. Override: the first flag or the configuration in the second file. In K8s: CoreDNS IP injected. Search domains added for cluster DNS resolution. Custom DNS useful for: corporate DNS servers, testing with custom domains.

questions.question: What is docker network inspect and what does it show?
questions.answer: Shows network configuration: subnet, gateway, connected containers, driver, options. Use to: debug connectivity issues (confirm containers on same network), see container IP addresses, verify DNS names. The first command lists all networks. The next commands add or remove containers from network at runtime.

questions.question: How do you debug a networking issue between two containers?
questions.answer: Verify both on same network: the first command — check Networks. Try by IP: the second command. Try by name: the third command. Check port: the fourth command. Check iptables: the fifth command. Use nicolaka/netshoot image for network debugging tools. Check firewall rules on host.

codeBlocks.code: docker exec c1 ping <ip of c2>

bestPractices: Use a specialized network troubleshooter image like nicolaka/netshoot for debugging.

questions.question: What happens to container networking when you restart Docker daemon?
questions.answer: Containers using bridge network: get new internal IPs on restart (unless fixed with the first option). User-defined networks persist but containers need restart. host network: unaffected. Port mappings are re-created. In production: don't rely on container IP addresses — always use DNS names or service discovery.
bestPractices: Don't rely on container IP addresses; always use DNS names or service discovery in production.

questions.question: What are the three types of Docker storage mounts?
questions.answer: Volume: managed by Docker, stored in /var/lib/docker/volumes — best for persistence. Bind mount: mounts host directory into container — best for dev (live code reload). tmpfs: in-memory only, not persisted — best for sensitive data in memory (secrets, temp files). Each has different use cases — don't use bind mounts in production containers.
warnings: Don't use bind mounts in production containers.

questions.question: What is a Docker volume and why is it preferred over bind mounts for production?
questions.answer: Volume: Docker-managed storage, isolated from host filesystem structure. Benefits: portable (no host path dependency), manageable (docker volume commands), shareable between containers, works on all platforms including Docker Desktop. Bind mounts: host-path dependent, permission issues, platform-specific paths. Named volumes in production always.
bestPractices: Always use named volumes in production for persistent data instead of bind mounts.

questions.question: How do you share a volume between containers?
questions.answer: Run the first command and the second command. Both containers read/write to same volume. Use for: sidecar patterns (log shipper reads app logs), init containers writing config, shared cache. Concurrent write risk: no built-in locking — application must handle concurrent access.
warnings: Concurrent write risk: there is no built-in locking; the application must handle concurrent access.

questions.question: What is the difference between docker volume create and anonymous volumes?
questions.answer: Named volume: the first command or the second parameter — persists after container removed, reusable, inspectable. Anonymous volume: the third parameter (no name) — Docker generates random name, removed with container if the fourth flag is used. Always use named volumes for data you care about — anonymous volumes are easy to lose.
bestPractices: Always use named volumes for data you care about.
warnings: Anonymous volumes are easy to lose because they can be deleted on container removal if not tracked.

questions.question: How do you backup a Docker volume?
questions.answer: Run the first command. This spins up a temporary container, tars volume contents to host. Restore by running the second command. No native backup command — this pattern is standard.

codeBlocks.code: docker run --rm -v myvol:/source -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar czf /backup/backup.tar.gz -C /source .
docker run --rm -v myvol:/target -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar xzf /backup/backup.tar.gz -C /target

questions.question: What happens to volume data when a container is deleted?
questions.answer: Named volumes: persist after container deletion — must delete volume separately (the first or second command). Anonymous volumes with the third flag: removed with container. Without the third flag: anonymous volume orphaned. The second command removes all unused volumes. Never use prune in production without checking what's there.
warnings: Never use docker volume prune in production without checking what volumes are actually there.

questions.question: What are volume drivers and when would you use them?
questions.answer: Plugins extending volume capabilities beyond local storage. Examples: rexray (cloud block storage), NFS driver (network share), S3 volume driver. Use for: shared volumes across hosts, cloud-native storage, specific performance requirements. In K8s: CSI drivers replace Docker volume drivers entirely — Docker volumes irrelevant in K8s.

questions.question: What is tmpfs mount and what is it used for?
questions.answer: In-memory filesystem — data never written to disk. Use for: sensitive data (tokens, passwords) that shouldn't be on disk, high-speed temporary storage, test fixtures. Run the following command. Data lost on container stop. In K8s: emptyDir with medium: Memory is equivalent. Good for secrets in memory rather than env vars.
bestPractices: Good for secrets in memory rather than env vars.

questions.question: How do you handle database data persistence with Docker?
questions.answer: Named volume for database data directory: the following option. Never use bind mount for DB data in production (permission issues, platform-specific). Backup volume regularly. For production: use managed database service (RDS) instead of containerised DB where possible. If containerised: dedicated persistent volume, no co-location with app.
bestPractices: For production, use a managed database service (like RDS) instead of a containerized database where possible.
If containerized, use a dedicated persistent volume and do not co-locate with the application.
warnings: Never use bind mounts for DB data in production due to permission and platform-specific issues.

questions.question: What is Docker Compose and what problem does it solve?
questions.answer: Tool for defining and running multi-container applications. The first file defines services, networks, volumes declaratively. A single command (the second command) starts entire application stack. Solves: complex commands like the third command with many flags, service startup ordering, shared network and volume config for local development.

codeBlocks.code:
# docker-compose.yml example
version: "3.8"
services:
  web:
    image: nginx

questions.question: What is the structure of a docker-compose.yml file?
questions.answer: Top-level keys: services (container definitions), networks (custom networks), volumes (named volumes). Each service: image or build, ports, environment, volumes, depends_on, networks, command, restart. version key: deprecated in Compose V2. Services automatically on shared default network — can reach each other by service name.

questions.question: What is the difference between docker-compose up and docker-compose run?
questions.answer: The first command starts all services defined in compose file, keeps running, shows logs. The second command runs a one-off command in a service container (doesn't start dependent services by default). Use it for: database migrations, one-time scripts, debugging. The third command option rebuilds images before starting. The fourth command option runs in detached mode (background).

questions.question: How does depends_on work in Docker Compose?
questions.answer: Controls startup order — waits for dependency container to start (not to be healthy). The option with the first condition waits for healthcheck to pass. The option with the second condition waits for one-shot service to exit 0. Note: application must still handle dependency unavailability — dependency order is not a guarantee the service is ready.
warnings: Application must still handle dependency unavailability; depends_on is not a guarantee that the service is actually ready.

questions.question: What is the difference between environment and env_file in Compose?
questions.answer: environment: inline env vars in compose file — visible in compose file (don't put secrets here). env_file: loads vars from a file (.env) — file not committed to Git. .env file: automatically loaded by Compose for variable substitution in compose file itself. Use env_file for local dev secrets. Never commit .env files.
bestPractices: Use env_file for local dev secrets.
Never commit .env files to Git.

questions.question: How do you scale a service in Docker Compose?
questions.answer: The following command runs 3 replicas of web service. Requires no host port mapping (or use range: '8080-8082:80'). Load balancer needed to distribute traffic across replicas. For production scaling: use K8s, not Compose — Compose not designed for production orchestration. Compose is a dev/test tool.
warnings: Compose is not designed for production orchestration; for production scaling, use Kubernetes.

questions.question: What is the build context in Docker Compose?
questions.answer: The first option specifies the path sent to Docker daemon as build context. The second option specifies the path to Dockerfile if not default. The third option specifies build arguments. The fourth option specifies images to use as cache source. In CI: build once, push to registry, reference by image in compose — don't build in production deployment. Build in CI, deploy image in prod.
bestPractices: In CI, build the image once, push it to a registry, and reference it via image name rather than building inside production deployments.

questions.question: How do you handle secrets in Docker Compose?
questions.answer: Compose secrets: top-level secrets key, mounted as files in /run/secrets/. More secure than environment variables (not visible in ps output). For dev: file-based secrets. For prod: Docker Swarm secrets or K8s Secrets. Never put production secrets in docker-compose.yml committed to Git. Use .env files for local dev only.
bestPractices: Use Docker Swarm secrets or Kubernetes Secrets in production.
Never put production secrets in docker-compose.yml committed to Git.

questions.question: What is override file in Docker Compose?
questions.answer: The first file is automatically merged with the second file. Use for: local dev overrides (mount source code, debug ports), CI overrides, environment-specific config. The third command allows explicit file merging. Base file: production-safe config. Override: dev-specific additions.

questions.question: What does docker compose down do vs docker compose stop?
questions.answer: The stop option stops running containers, preserves containers and volumes. The down option stops AND removes containers and default networks. The third option also removes volumes (DANGER — deletes data). The fourth option also removes images. Use stop for temporary pause, down for full teardown. Never run the third option in production — data loss.
warnings: Never run docker compose down -v in production; it deletes volume data.

questions.question: What are the main Docker security concerns?
questions.answer: Container escape (breakout to host). Privileged containers (full host access). Root processes in containers. Image vulnerabilities (outdated base images). Exposed Docker socket (gives root access to host). Secrets in images or env vars. Unrestricted resource usage. Each requires different mitigation — defence in depth.

questions.question: What does running a container as root mean and why is it dangerous?
questions.answer: By default containers run as root (UID 0). If container escapes namespace (CVE), process has root on host. Root in container can: write to mounted volumes, access sensitive host paths, exhaust resources. Fix: the USER instruction in Dockerfile (run as non-root UID). K8s: the following options in securityContext.
bestPractices: Always run containers as non-root using the USER instruction in Dockerfile.
Enforce runAsNonRoot in Kubernetes securityContext.

questions.question: What is a privileged container and when would you ever use it?
questions.answer: The first flag gives container nearly all host capabilities — can access devices, modify kernel parameters, see all host processes. Essentially root on the host. Avoid in production. Legitimate uses: Docker-in-Docker (CI runners), network tools needing raw sockets, kernel module loading. Always prefer specific options with the second flag over the first flag.
bestPractices: Always prefer specific --cap-add flags over --privileged.
warnings: Avoid using privileged containers in production.

questions.question: What are Linux capabilities in Docker context?
questions.answer: Root privileges split into ~40 capabilities (CAP_NET_ADMIN, CAP_SYS_PTRACE, etc). Docker drops most by default. Use the first option to add a specific capability. Or the second and third options for minimal privilege. Never add capabilities without understanding what they allow. In K8s: use the following configuration in securityContext capabilities.
bestPractices: For minimal privilege, drop all capabilities and then add only specific required ones.
warnings: Never add capabilities without understanding what security implications they carry.

questions.question: What is the Docker socket and why is it a security risk?
questions.answer: Unix socket at /var/run/docker.sock. Mounting socket into container: the following option gives container full Docker daemon access — equivalent to root on host. Any container with socket access can: start privileged containers, mount host filesystem, escape to host. Never mount socket in production containers.
warnings: Never mount the Docker socket (/var/run/docker.sock) in production containers as it gives full root-level control over the host.

questions.question: How do you scan Docker images for vulnerabilities?
questions.answer: Trivy command: the following. Fast, open source, scans OS packages + app dependencies. Integrate in CI: fail build on CRITICAL or HIGH CVEs. ECR enhanced scanning: automatic on push. Snyk, Clair, Grype: alternatives. Scan base images AND final images. Rescan periodically — new CVEs discovered against old images.
bestPractices: Integrate image scanning in CI/CD pipelines to fail builds on CRITICAL/HIGH CVEs.
Rescan base images and final images periodically.

questions.question: What is a read-only filesystem for containers?
questions.answer: The first command mounts container filesystem read-only. Process can't write to filesystem — prevents malware persistence, accidental file modification. Combine with the second option for writable temp space. In K8s: the third option in securityContext. Forces explicit volume mounts for all writable paths — improves security posture significantly.
bestPractices: Mount container filesystem read-only and combine with a tmpfs for temp directories to prevent malware persistence.

questions.question: What is seccomp in Docker?
questions.answer: Secure Computing Mode: filters syscalls available to container. Docker's default seccomp profile blocks ~44 dangerous syscalls (reboot, mount, etc). Custom profile: allow only syscalls your app needs. The following option specifies it. Most apps work fine with default profile. Distroless + seccomp + read-only filesystem: strong hardening combination.
bestPractices: Combine distroless base images, custom or default seccomp profiles, and a read-only filesystem for the strongest container hardening.

questions.question: What is AppArmor/SELinux in Docker context?
questions.answer: Mandatory Access Control. AppArmor (Ubuntu): profile restricts file access, capabilities, network. docker-default AppArmor profile applied automatically. SELinux (RHEL/CentOS): label-based, confines processes to specific contexts. Both add defence-in-depth beyond namespaces and capabilities. On EKS: nodes have SELinux — understand implications for volume mounts.

questions.question: How do you prevent container image supply chain attacks?
questions.answer: Use minimal, verified base images (official Docker images, distroless). Pin exact digest: the first format, not the second. Sign images with Docker Content Trust (DCT) or Cosign (sigstore). Scan images in CI. Private registry — don't pull from public registries at deploy time. SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) generation. Review Dockerfile carefully before using.
bestPractices: Pin exact image digests in production.
Generate SBOMs.
Review Dockerfiles carefully before execution.

questions.question: What is Docker Content Trust (DCT)?
questions.answer: The following environment variable enables image signing and verification. Publisher signs image with private key. Pull verifies signature — refuses unsigned or tampered images. Uses Notary under the hood. Cosign (sigstore): modern replacement, integrates with OCI registries better. In regulated environments: require signed images via admission webhook.

questions.question: How do you set CPU limits for a Docker container?
questions.answer: The first option limits container to max 0.5 CPU cores. The second option sets relative weight (default 1024) — affects scheduling when contention. The third option pins to specific CPU cores. In K8s: use the fourth option. Always set CPU limits in production — without them one container can starve others. CPU throttled at limit, not killed.
bestPractices: Always set CPU limits in production to prevent resource starvation.

questions.question: How do you set memory limits and what happens when exceeded?
questions.answer: The first option sets hard limit. The second option sets soft limit (scheduling hint). The third option sets swap limit. When container exceeds memory limit: OOM killer terminates the process (not the container — container may restart per restart policy). In K8s: container OOMKilled, kubelet restarts. Always set memory limits in production.
bestPractices: Always set memory limits in production.
warnings: Exceeding memory limits triggers the kernel OOM killer to terminate the container processes.

questions.question: What is the difference between CPU limit and CPU reservation in Docker?
questions.answer: The first option (limit) is a hard cap — container never gets more. The second option (reservation/weight) affects scheduling priority during contention only. If host not under pressure: container can use more than its share. K8s equivalent: requests = reservation (scheduling), limits = hard cap. Always set both requests and limits in K8s.
bestPractices: Always set both requests and limits in Kubernetes configuration.

questions.question: How do you monitor Docker container resource usage?
questions.answer: The first command displays live CPU, memory, network I/O, block I/O per container. The second command takes a single snapshot. cAdvisor is a container metrics exporter for Prometheus — scrapes the third path. In K8s: metrics-server + the fourth command. Grafana dashboards with cAdvisor + Prometheus: standard production monitoring stack.

questions.question: What is the --restart policy in Docker?
questions.answer: no (default): never restart. The first option restarts on non-zero exit, with optional max attempts. The second option always restarts including after daemon restart. The third option is like always but not if manually stopped. Use: on-failure for production services. In K8s: RestartPolicy on pod (Always, OnFailure, Never) — different mechanism.
bestPractices: Use on-failure restart policy for production microservices.

questions.question: How do you handle Docker log management to prevent disk exhaustion?
questions.answer: Default json-file driver: logs accumulate indefinitely. Set limits with the first option in the second file or per container. Log drivers: json-file, syslog, journald, fluentd, awslogs (CloudWatch). In K8s: configure log rotation in kubelet config. Ship logs to centralised system (Loki, CloudWatch) — don't rely on container logs on disk.
bestPractices: Ship logs to a centralized system (Loki, CloudWatch, etc.) rather than relying on on-disk files.
warnings: The default json-file log driver allows logs to accumulate indefinitely, risking host disk exhaustion.

questions.question: What is Docker image layer caching and how does it affect CI build speed?
questions.answer: Layers cached on builder host — consecutive builds reuse unchanged layers. In CI (ephemeral runners): no local cache between runs. Solutions: the first option to pull cache from registry, BuildKit inline cache, GitHub Actions cache action for the second path. Multi-stage builds reduce layers needing transfer. Proper Dockerfile layer ordering critical.
bestPractices: Maintain proper Dockerfile layer ordering.
Use --cache-from registry pull-through or BuildKit remote cache in CI.

questions.question: What is BuildKit and what does it add over classic Docker build?
questions.answer: BuildKit: modern build engine replacing legacy builder. Features: parallel stage execution (multi-stage faster), cache mounts (persist package manager cache across builds), secret mounts (secrets not in image layers), SSH mounts, better cache invalidation, the first option. Enable: the second environment variable or buildx. Default in Docker 23+.

questions.question: How do you profile and debug a slow Docker build?
questions.answer: The first command shows timing for each step. Identify slow steps: network downloads, large COPY, slow compilation. Solutions: better layer ordering (cache deps before code), BuildKit cache mounts for package managers, multi-stage (skip unnecessary work in final stage), smaller base image, pre-built dependency layer. Use dive tool to analyse layer sizes.
bestPractices: Analyze layer sizes and file leakage using the dive tool.
Leverage BuildKit cache mounts for dependency managers.

questions.question: How do you build and push a Docker image in GitHub Actions?
questions.answer: Login: the first command (or docker/login-action). Build: the second command. Tag with git SHA for traceability. Push: the third command. Use OIDC with AWS — no stored credentials. Build once per commit. Tag both :commit-sha and :latest (or :branch). Cache with the fourth option from previous image.
bestPractices: Use OIDC with cloud providers to avoid storing long-lived credentials in GitHub Actions.
Build once per commit and promotion retag instead of rebuilding.

questions.question: What is Docker Buildx and why use it?
questions.answer: Extended build capabilities: multi-platform builds, BuildKit features, remote builders. The following command builds for multiple architectures simultaneously. Needed for: Apple Silicon dev machines building for AMD64 servers, ARM-based K8s nodes. Manifest list in registry: single tag, Docker pulls correct arch.

questions.question: What is Docker-in-Docker (DinD) and what are the alternatives?
questions.answer: DinD: run Docker daemon inside a container (privileged). Used in CI for building images. Problems: privileged container (security risk), cache not shared between builds, volume mount issues. Alternatives: Kaniko (builds images in unprivileged container, no daemon), Buildah, img. In K8s CI: Kaniko preferred over DinD for security.
bestPractices: Use Kaniko or Buildah in Kubernetes CI instead of Docker-in-Docker to eliminate privileged container dependencies.

questions.question: How do you tag Docker images effectively?
questions.answer: Never rely on latest in production — it's mutable. Tag with: git commit SHA (immutable, traceable), semantic version (v1.2.3 for releases), branch name (mutable, for dev). Pattern: the first format for production, the second format for CI artifacts. Use the third format for absolute immutability. Scan before pushing — don't push unscanned images.
bestPractices: Tag using git commit SHA, semantic versioning, and secure digests for deployment verification.
Scan images before pushing.
warnings: Never rely on the latest tag in production since it is mutable.

questions.question: What is a multi-platform Docker image?
questions.answer: Single image tag that works on multiple CPU architectures (amd64, arm64). Docker manifest list: tag points to manifest listing platform-specific image digests. Docker pulls correct one automatically. Build with the following command option. Required for: ARM-based cloud instances (Graviton), Apple Silicon developers. Single tag in K8s works across mixed node architectures.

questions.question: How do you reduce CI build time for Docker images?
questions.answer: Layer cache optimisation (deps before code). BuildKit the first option for npm/pip/Maven caches. The second option from registry image (pull cache from previous build). Parallel multi-stage execution with BuildKit. Smaller base images (alpine) = less to pull. Remote build cache (Depot, BuildKit remote cache). Pre-built dependency layers updated on dependency changes only.
bestPractices: Cache package manager dependencies using BuildKit cache mounts.
Use minimal base images to reduce pull times.

questions.question: How do you implement image promotion across environments?
questions.answer: Build once, promote same image across dev/staging/prod. Tag: the first format (built in CI). Promote: retag for environment (the second format) or use digest. Never rebuild image for production — same bits tested in staging go to prod. Scan in CI before dev promotion. No production build from source — only already-tested images promoted.
warnings: Never rebuild images for production from source; promote the same already-tested image artifact instead.

questions.question: What is Kaniko and when do you use it?
questions.answer: Builds Docker images inside Kubernetes without Docker daemon. No privileged container required. Reads Dockerfile, builds in userspace, pushes to registry. Use in: K8s-based CI (Tekton, Argo Workflows), environments where DinD is prohibited. Slightly slower than daemon-based builds. Security: no daemon socket, no privileged mode required.

questions.question: How do you handle Docker image vulnerability remediation in CI?
questions.answer: Trivy in CI: fail pipeline on CRITICAL CVEs (configurable threshold). Base image pinned to digest — no surprise updates. Weekly automated PR to bump base image version. Separate pipeline to rescan existing production images against new CVE database. Dependency update tools (Renovate, Dependabot) for app dependencies. Track CVE remediation SLA by severity.
bestPractices: Pin base images to specific digests.
Implement weekly automated PRs to bump base images.
Set up a separate vulnerability rescan pipeline for production images.

questions.question: A container exits immediately after docker run — how do you debug?
questions.answer: The first command shows stopped containers. The second command shows output before exit. The third command checks ExitCode (0=success, 1=app error, 137=OOMKill/SIGKILL, 139=segfault, 143=SIGTERM). Run interactively: the fourth command — override CMD. Check ENTRYPOINT — may be pointing to non-existent binary.

questions.question: How do you debug a running container?
questions.answer: The first command starts an interactive shell. The second command follows logs. The third command shows running processes. The fourth command shows resource usage. The fifth command shows full config and state. If no shell in distroless: the sixth command (Docker Desktop) or the seventh command in K8s. Use the eighth command on host for low-level debugging.

questions.question: A container can't connect to another container — debug steps?
questions.answer: The first two commands confirm both are on same network. Test by name: the third command. DNS resolution: the fourth command. Test port: the fifth command. Check: containers on same user-defined network (not default bridge), correct container names, correct port, no firewall rules blocking.

questions.question: How do you investigate high memory usage in a container?
questions.answer: The first command shows current memory usage vs limit. The second command reads meminfo. Check for memory leak: graph memory over time in Grafana/cAdvisor. OOMKill check: the third command — look at OOMKilled in State. In K8s: the fourth command — see OOMKilled events. Heap dump for JVM apps. Application profiling (like the fifth command for Python).

questions.question: How do you recover from a corrupted Docker installation?
questions.answer: Symptoms: daemon not starting, containers in bad state. Steps: the first command. If fails: check the second command. Nuclear option: stop docker, remove the third path (DESTROYS ALL DATA), restart docker. On EKS: node replacement preferred over recovery. Always have data in volumes outside the third path — don't store important data in container writable layer.
bestPractices: Always store important data in volumes outside /var/lib/docker.
warnings: Removing /var/lib/docker DESTROYS ALL DATA.
Do not store important data in the container writable layer.

questions.question: What does 'Error response from daemon: No space left on device' mean?
questions.answer: Docker disk exhaustion. Check: the first command (disk), the second command (Docker disk usage breakdown). Clean up: the third command (remove unused images), the fourth command, the fifth command, the sixth command. Set log rotation limits. On EKS nodes: node disk pressure — kubelet evicts pods. Prevent: set log limits, prune regularly, monitor disk usage.
bestPractices: Set log rotation limits and prune regularly to avoid disk exhaustion.

questions.question: How do you debug a container that won't stop (stuck in stopping)?
questions.answer: The first command sends SIGTERM, waits 10s (configurable with the second option), then SIGKILL. If stuck after kill: zombie process or kernel issue. The third command forces kill. If still stuck: check for docker daemon issues. On K8s: kubelet handles SIGTERM → grace period → SIGKILL. Ensure the app handles SIGTERM gracefully with a preStop hook.
bestPractices: Ensure the application handles SIGTERM gracefully to avoid abrupt process termination.
In Kubernetes, use a preStop hook if needed.

questions.question: What does 'cannot allocate memory in static TLS block' error mean?
questions.answer: glibc issue with certain shared libraries loaded after process start (common with Python + numpy/torch). Fix: preload the library using the first assignment. Or use a different base image. Or set the second environment variable in Dockerfile ENV. Not a Docker bug — glibc/dynamic linker behaviour.

questions.question: How do you debug image pull failures?
questions.answer: 'Manifest unknown': wrong tag or image doesn't exist. 'unauthorized': auth failed — re-run the first command or check credentials. 'timeout': network issue or registry unavailable. Rate limiting (Docker Hub): authenticated pulls have higher limits. In K8s: check the second configuration option on pod, verify secret has correct registry credentials. ECR: token expires every 12h — use credential helper.
warnings: ECR tokens expire every 12 hours; use the credential helper to handle renewal automatically.

questions.question: How do you trace which process inside a container is causing high CPU?
questions.answer: The first command or the second command shows processes. The third command shows container-level CPU. On host: the second command sorted by CPU, check PIDs — Docker container PIDs visible on host (shared kernel). Use the fourth command to enter container namespace from host. Use the fifth, sixth, or seventh tools for application-level profiling. cAdvisor for container-level metrics.

questions.question: Design a Docker-based CI/CD pipeline for a Node.js microservice.
questions.answer: GitHub Actions: checkout → docker build (multi-stage: test stage runs tests, prod stage builds artifact) → Trivy scan (fail on CRITICAL) → docker push to ECR with git SHA tag → ArgoCD updates image tag in Git → K8s pulls new image. No Docker daemon in K8s CI: use Kaniko or GitHub-hosted runner. Cache: the first option from previous tag.
bestPractices: Build once and promote/retag images to ensure environmental alignment.
In Kubernetes-based CI/CD where DinD is restricted, build images with Kaniko.

questions.question: A Docker image in production is 2.3GB — how do you reduce it?
questions.answer: Audit with dive tool: see layer-by-layer size. Replace base image with alpine or distroless. Multi-stage build: only copy compiled artifact to final stage. Remove: dev dependencies (using the first command), test files, documentation, cache files (.apt, .npm, .pip). Chain RUN commands with cleanup. Target: under 200MB for most Node.js apps.
bestPractices: Use alpine or distroless base images.
Utilize multi-stage builds.
Clean up dependencies and cache files in the same RUN layer to keep size under 200MB.

questions.question: How would you migrate a legacy application into Docker?
questions.answer: Understand: dependencies, config sources, data persistence, ports, startup sequence. Write Dockerfile: appropriate base image, COPY app, install deps, set CMD. Externalise config: env vars not hardcoded. Volumes for persistent data. Health endpoint. Test: run locally, verify behaviour matches bare-metal. Multi-stage if compilation needed. Then containerise, don't 'Dockerise' — rethink where needed.

questions.question: Your containerised app works locally but fails in production K8s — why might that happen?
questions.answer: Common causes: different env vars (check ConfigMap/Secret). Resource limits too low (OOMKill, CPU throttling). Read-only filesystem (K8s security policy). Non-root user (file permission issues). Different network topology (service DNS vs localhost). Image pull issues (private registry, wrong tag). Security context (capabilities dropped). Always test with K8s-matching security context locally.
bestPractices: Always test container configurations locally with a security context that matches production Kubernetes settings.

questions.question: How do you handle config management for containers across environments?
questions.answer: 12-factor app: config from environment variables. K8s: ConfigMap for non-sensitive, Secret for sensitive — both mounted as env vars or files. Never bake environment-specific config into image — same image across all environments, config injected at runtime. Validate required env vars at container startup — fail fast with clear error if missing.
bestPractices: Never bake environment-specific configuration into the container image.
Inject config at runtime via environment variables, ConfigMaps, or Secrets.

questions.question: Design a secure container runtime environment for a financial services company.
questions.answer: Non-root containers (using the first setting). Read-only root filesystem. Drop ALL capabilities, add only required. Seccomp profile. AppArmor/SELinux enforced. No privileged containers. Network policies (deny all, allow specific). Image scanning (Trivy + Snyk) in CI. Admission controller (OPA Gatekeeper) enforces policies. No Docker socket mounts. Immutable tags only. SBOM for all images. Regular base image updates.
bestPractices: Enforce non-root execution, read-only filesystems, minimal capabilities, admission controllers, and regular base image updates for highly secure environments.

questions.question: How do you handle graceful shutdown of a containerised application?
questions.answer: App must handle SIGTERM: close connections, finish in-flight requests, save state, exit cleanly. K8s: sends SIGTERM, waits the first setting (default 30s), then SIGKILL. preStop hook: add the second command to allow load balancer to deregister before SIGTERM. Node.js: the third snippet. Don't trap SIGKILL. Test graceful shutdown explicitly.
bestPractices: Implement custom SIGTERM handlers to gracefully close connections.
Use preStop sleep hooks in Kubernetes if load balancers need extra time to deregister.

questions.question: How would you containerise a machine learning model serving application?
questions.answer: Base image: the first image or the second image for GPU. Multi-stage: dependency install stage (using the third command) cached separately. Model weights: NOT in image — mount from volume or download at startup from S3. GPU: the fourth flag or K8s nvidia device plugin. Memory limits: size for model + overhead. Health check: the fifth endpoint checks model loaded. Startup probe for slow model loading.
bestPractices: Do not store heavy model weights inside the Docker image; pull them from external storage (S3) or mount via volumes at startup.

questions.question: If you had to redesign your Docker strategy from scratch, what would you change?
questions.answer: Multi-stage builds from day one — single-stage is technical debt. Distroless base images immediately — smaller and more secure. Pin exact base image digests — no surprise updates. Non-root USER in every Dockerfile. Read-only filesystem by default. Image scanning in every CI pipeline with hard failure on CRITICAL. BuildKit always — better caching, secret mounts, parallel stages. SBOM generation automated. The best container is the smallest one that runs your app correctly.
bestPractices: Adopt multi-stage builds from day one.
Use distroless images, non-root users, and read-only filesystems by default.
Automate SBOM generation and image scanning in CI/CD.
